newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Hopes grow for direct Taiwan-China sailings.
newsitem.headline: Hopes grow for direct Taiwan-China sailings.

text.p: Taiwan state radio on Thursday said arch rival China's Fujian province had given preliminary approval for four Taiwan firms to sail across the Taiwan strait -- portending the first direct crossings since 1949.
The broadcast, which did not name its sources, said the applications to sail between Taiwan and Fujian's Xiamen port had been sent to the communist central government for review.
Taiwan media on Thursday said local shipping leaders had begun receiving invitations for an April 8 ceremony in Xiamen to mark the first direct crossing.
Xiamen officials declined to comment on the reports.
Taiwan state radio said at least four shippers -- Yangming Marine Transport Corp, Uniglory Marine, Wan Hai Lines and Chinese Marltime Transport Ltd -- had won approval from Fujian province.

Yangming, a global giant, said it expected to know by early April the fate of its application, which if approved could yield transport savings of US$26 million a year. "We're confident that Yangming will be among those getting permission for cross-strait shipping," Yangming spokesman M.S. Tsay told Reuters.
The director of the transport and communications ministry's navigation department, Shieh Ming-hui, told state radio that he could not comment on China's processing of the applications.
As for Chinese requests to sail into Taiwan ports, Shieh said none had been received but added that such applications could be processed within a week.
Other ministry officials cautiously reiterated the island's terms for direct links, seeking to ensure a breakthrough did not undermine the sovereignty of Taiwan's exiled Republic of China.
Taiwan was ready to receive ships sailing from China as long as they were owned by mainland, Taiwan or Hong Kong interests and flew a Hong Kong or third-country flag, they said.
Officials stressed that under current rules cargoes arriving directly from China could enter Taiwan's Kaohsiung port but would not be allowed to pass through Taiwan customs.

Taiwan has banned direct links since 1949, when the island was separated from the newly communist mainland by a civil war, though indirect trade and Taiwan investment in the mainland have flourished since a political thaw began in the late 1980s.

Facing intense pressure to ease the ban, Taipei has proposed an "offshore transshipment centre" where incoming mainland cargoes could be processed in bonded zones outside Taiwan customs for onward international shipment.

Taking a different tack, Beijing maintains that since Taiwan is part of China, cross-strait shipping is a domestic issue that initially should involve mainland, Taiwan or Hong Kong ships or foreign-flagged ships that are wholly or partially owned by mainland, Taiwan or Hong Kong interests.
Beijing has made no public response to Taiwan's proposal, which strives to preserve the Republic of China's sovereignty by not giving berth to ships flying communist China's flag.
Likewise, Beijing would spurn any ship flying the republican flag as this would contravene its "one China" principle.
On February 23, the Hong Kong container ship Lien Fung made what experts called the first quasi-direct crossing, passing through Hong Kong harbour en route to Kaohsiung from Xiamen.

That unprecedented passage and several since, widely seen as an incremental easing of Taiwan's ban, was possible under a pact reached in Hong Kong on January 22 by Taiwan and China shipping executives with tacit approval of both governments.
